title: Physics: Energy, Electricity and Electromagnetism – Criterion A Paper

questions.text: Define work done.
questions.markScheme: Work done is the product of the force and the distance moved in the direction of the force ($W = Fd$)

questions.text: Outline the two conditions needed for work to be done on an object.
questions.markScheme: A force must act on the object; the object must move in the direction of (a component of) the force

questions.context: A crate is pulled 12 m along a horizontal floor by a rope. The tension in the rope is 150 N and the rope makes an angle of 30° above the horizontal.
questions.text: Calculate the work done by the rope on the crate.
questions.markScheme: Horizontal component of force $= 150\cos 30° = 130$ N; $W = 130 \times 12$; $W = 1.56 \times 10^{3}$ J

questions.context: A student carries a bag at constant height while walking horizontally across a room.
questions.text: Explain why the upward force of the student's arm does no work on the bag.
questions.markScheme: The force is vertical but the displacement is horizontal / angle between force and motion is 90°; so no movement in the direction of the force, $W = Fd\cos 90° = 0$

questions.text: State four different forms (stores) of energy.
questions.markScheme: Any four from: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, chemical, thermal, nuclear, electrical, light, sound, magnetic; 1 mark for every two correct

questions.context: A roller-coaster car of mass 500 kg starts at rest at the top of a hill 32 m high. Assume no friction. Take $g = 9.81$ N kg$^{-1}$.
questions.text: Calculate the speed of the car at the bottom of the hill.
questions.markScheme: $E_p = mgh = 500 \times 9.81 \times 32 = 1.57 \times 10^{5}$ J; $E_k$ at bottom = $E_p$ / $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = mgh$; $v = \sqrt{2gh} = 25.1$ m s$^{-1}$

questions.context: In reality the car in 2b reaches the bottom of the hill at 22 m s$^{-1}$.
questions.text: Calculate the energy transferred to thermal energy by friction and air resistance.
questions.markScheme: $E_k = \frac{1}{2} \times 500 \times 22^{2} = 1.21 \times 10^{5}$ J; energy lost $= 1.57 \times 10^{5} - 1.21 \times 10^{5} = 3.60 \times 10^{4}$ J (ECF from 2b)

questions.context: A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 15 m s$^{-1}$ collides with a stationary car of mass 800 kg. The two cars stick together.
questions.text: Calculate the velocity of the cars immediately after the collision.
questions.markScheme: Momentum before $= 1200 \times 15 = 1.8 \times 10^{4}$ kg m s$^{-1}$; momentum conserved, total mass $= 2000$ kg; $v = 9.0$ m s$^{-1}$

questions.text: Determine the kinetic energy lost in the collision in 2d.
questions.markScheme: $E_k$ before $= 1.35 \times 10^{5}$ J and after $= 8.1 \times 10^{4}$ J; loss $= 5.4 \times 10^{4}$ J

questions.text: Explain why momentum is conserved in the collision in 2d but kinetic energy is not.
questions.markScheme: No external resultant force acts, so total momentum of the isolated system is conserved; the collision is inelastic: kinetic energy is transferred to thermal, sound and deformation (total energy is still conserved)

questions.context: A filament lamp has an input of 60 J every second. It transfers 9 J per second as light and the rest as thermal energy.
questions.text: Construct a labelled Sankey diagram for the lamp and calculate its efficiency.
questions.markScheme: Input arrow labelled 60 J splitting into light 9 J and thermal 51 J; arrow widths drawn to scale / proportional; efficiency $= 9/60 \times 100 = 15\%$

questions.text: Distinguish between renewable and non-renewable energy resources.
questions.markScheme: Renewable: replenished naturally on a human timescale / will not run out (e.g. solar, wind); non-renewable: finite, used faster than it is replaced (e.g. coal, oil, gas, uranium)

questions.text: Compare solar panels and coal-fired power stations as ways of generating electricity.
questions.markScheme: Solar is renewable, coal is non-renewable; solar emits no CO2 when operating, coal releases CO2/greenhouse gases and pollutants; coal is reliable/controllable (baseload), solar is intermittent (no output at night/cloud); solar has low running costs but needs large land area/high set-up cost, coal has fuel costs but high power output per site; 1 mark per valid comparison, both sides needed

questions.context: A student of mass 65 kg runs up a flight of stairs with a vertical height of 4.0 m in 5.0 s.
questions.text: Calculate the useful power developed by the student.
questions.markScheme: Work $= mgh = 65 \times 9.81 \times 4.0 = 2.55 \times 10^{3}$ J; $P = W/t = 510$ W

questions.context: An electric motor with an input power of 800 W lifts a 50 kg load through a vertical height of 6.0 m in 6.0 s.
questions.text: Calculate the efficiency of the motor.
questions.markScheme: Useful energy $= 50 \times 9.81 \times 6.0 = 2.94 \times 10^{3}$ J; useful power $= 2943/6.0 = 491$ W; efficiency $= 491/800 \times 100 = 61.3\%$

questions.text: Explain, in terms of electrons, why a polythene rod becomes negatively charged when rubbed with a woollen cloth.
questions.markScheme: Friction transfers electrons from the wool to the polythene (polythene holds electrons more tightly); polythene gains electrons so is negative, wool loses an equal number and is equally positive

questions.context: A neutral metal sphere stands on an insulating stand. A positively charged rod is available.
questions.text: Describe how the sphere can be given a negative charge by induction, without the rod touching it.
questions.markScheme: Bring the positive rod near: electrons attracted to the near side; earth the sphere: electrons flow from earth onto the sphere; remove the earth connection first, then the rod, leaving the sphere negative

questions.context: Two small charged spheres of +2.0 μC and −6.0 μC are placed 5.0 cm apart. $k = 8.99 \times 10^{9}$ N m$^{2}$ C$^{-2}$.
questions.text: Calculate the electrostatic force between the spheres and state its direction.
questions.markScheme: $F = \frac{8.99 \times 10^{9} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 6.0 \times 10^{-6}}{0.050^{2}}$ (units converted); $F = 43.2$ N; attractive (unlike charges)

questions.text: Describe the electric field pattern between a positive and a negative point charge.
questions.markScheme: Field lines start on the positive charge and end on the negative charge, with arrows from + to −; lines never cross and are closest together (field strongest) between and near the charges

questions.context: A current of 0.40 A flows through a lamp for 5.0 minutes. The potential difference across the lamp is 6.0 V.
questions.text: Calculate the charge that flows through the lamp.
Calculate the energy transferred by the lamp in 6a.

questions.context: A nichrome wire is 1.5 m long with a diameter of 0.30 mm. The resistivity of nichrome is $1.1 \times 10^{-6}$ Ω m.
questions.text: Calculate the resistance of the wire.
Explain why the I–V graph of a filament lamp is a curve and not a straight line.
questions.markScheme: As current increases the filament temperature rises; metal ions vibrate with larger amplitude so electrons collide with them more often; resistance increases so current increases less for each extra volt (not proportional, non-ohmic)

questions.context: At 12 V a filament lamp draws a current of 0.50 A.
questions.text: Determine the resistance of the lamp at 12 V and explain why the gradient of the I–V graph cannot be used.
questions.markScheme: $R = V/I = 12/0.50 = 24$ Ω; resistance is V/I at that point; the I–V graph is curved so its gradient is not R (for a straight I–V line the gradient is 1/R)

questions.context: A 6.0 Ω resistor is connected in series with a parallel pair of 4.0 Ω and 12 Ω resistors. The combination is connected to an 18 V supply of negligible internal resistance.
questions.text: Calculate the total current drawn from the supply.
questions.markScheme: Parallel pair $= (4.0 \times 12)/16 = 3.0$ Ω, total $= 9.0$ Ω; $I = 18/9.0 = 2.0$ A

questions.text: Calculate the current in the 4.0 Ω resistor in 7a.
questions.markScheme: pd across pair $= 2.0 \times 3.0 = 6.0$ V; $I = 6.0/4.0 = 1.5$ A

questions.context: A light sensor uses a 9.0 V supply, a fixed 10 kΩ resistor and an LDR in series. The output pd $V_{out}$ is taken across the LDR. The LDR's resistance is 50 kΩ in the dark and 2.5 kΩ in bright light.
questions.text: Calculate $V_{out}$ in the dark and in bright light.
questions.markScheme: $V_{out} = V_{in} \times R_{LDR}/(R_{fixed} + R_{LDR})$; dark: $9.0 \times 50/60 = 7.5$ V; bright: $9.0 \times 2.5/12.5 = 1.8$ V

questions.text: Draw a circuit diagram of the light sensor in 7c, including a voltmeter measuring $V_{out}$.
questions.markScheme: Cell, fixed resistor and LDR in one series loop with correct symbols (LDR: resistor in circle with arrows pointing in); voltmeter connected in parallel across the LDR only

questions.context: A 1.5 kW heater is connected to the 230 V mains. Fuses of 3 A, 5 A and 13 A are available.
questions.text: Calculate the normal operating current and choose the most suitable fuse.
questions.markScheme: $I = P/V = 1500/230 = 6.52$ A; 13 A fuse (smallest rating above the operating current)

questions.context: The heater in 8a has a metal case. A fault causes the live wire to touch the case.
questions.text: Explain how the earth wire and the fuse together protect the user.
questions.markScheme: Earth wire provides a low-resistance path from the case to earth; a very large current flows from live to earth; current exceeds the fuse rating, the fuse melts and disconnects the live wire, so the case does not stay live

questions.text: Explain why a residual current device (RCD) protects a person from electric shock better than a fuse.
questions.markScheme: A fatal shock needs only tens of milliamps, far below a fuse rating so a fuse would not blow; an RCD detects a small difference (about 30 mA) between live and neutral currents and cuts the supply within milliseconds

questions.context: A power station transmits 80 MW at 200 kV through lines with a total resistance of 6.0 Ω.
questions.text: Calculate the power lost in the lines as a percentage of the power transmitted.
Outline three ways in which a smart grid helps a country use more sustainable energy.
questions.markScheme: Smart meters and time-of-use tariffs shift demand away from peaks (demand response); energy storage absorbs surplus solar/wind and releases it later; two-way flow allows distributed generation such as rooftop solar; real-time data/forecasting balances variable renewables; reduced losses and theft; any three, 1 mark each

questions.text: State the law of magnetic poles.
questions.markScheme: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract

questions.text: Explain, using domain theory, how an iron bar becomes magnetised when placed in a magnetic field.
questions.markScheme: In unmagnetised iron the domains point in random directions so their fields cancel; in the field the domains align (aligned domains grow / others rotate) in the same direction, so their fields add and the bar becomes a magnet

questions.text: Describe the magnetic field around a long straight wire carrying a current.
questions.markScheme: Concentric circles centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it; circles further apart with increasing distance (field weaker); direction given by the right-hand grip rule and reverses if the current reverses

questions.text: State two ways to increase the strength of an electromagnet made from a solenoid.
questions.markScheme: Any two: increase the current; increase the number of turns (per unit length); add a soft-iron core

questions.context: A straight wire of length 0.25 m carries a current of 3.0 A at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.40 T.
questions.text: Calculate the force on the wire.

questions.context: The coil of a DC motor has 50 turns. Each side of the coil in the field is 4.0 cm long. The flux density is 0.20 T and the current is 1.5 A.
questions.text: Calculate the force on one side of the coil.
questions.markScheme: $F = NBIL = 50 \times 0.20 \times 1.5 \times 0.040$; $F = 0.60$ N

questions.text: Explain the purpose of the split-ring commutator in a DC motor.
questions.markScheme: It reverses the current in the coil every half turn; this happens as the coil passes the vertical position, so the force on each side reverses as it moves to the other pole; the turning effect therefore stays in the same direction and the coil keeps rotating one way

questions.context: In the DC motor construction lab, a coil of enamelled wire rests on paper-clip supports over a magnet. The enamel is stripped completely from one end of the axle, but only from the top half of the other end.
questions.text: Explain why one end of the axle is only half stripped.
questions.markScheme: Current flows only during half of each turn (when bare copper touches the support); during that half the force turns the coil in one direction; for the other half there is no current and no opposing force, so the coil coasts round on its momentum (acts as a simple commutator)

questions.context: A bar magnet is moved relative to a coil connected to a centre-zero galvanometer.
questions.text: Describe what the galvanometer shows when the N pole is (i) pushed into the coil, (ii) held still inside it, (iii) pulled out quickly.
questions.markScheme: (i) needle deflects one way; (ii) reads zero because the flux is not changing; (iii) deflects the opposite way and further / larger deflection because flux changes faster

questions.text: State Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction and outline how a dynamic microphone uses electromagnetic induction.
questions.markScheme: Induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage; sound waves make the diaphragm and attached coil vibrate in the field of a permanent magnet; the changing flux induces an alternating emf that copies the sound wave

questions.text: Explain how Lenz's law is a consequence of the conservation of energy.
questions.markScheme: The induced current opposes the change/motion, so work must be done to move the magnet and this work becomes electrical energy; if it aided the motion, energy would be created from nothing, violating conservation of energy

questions.context: The mains supply in India is 230 V rms at 50 Hz.
questions.text: Calculate the peak voltage and the period of the supply.
Explain how an AC generator produces an alternating emf.
questions.markScheme: Coil rotates in a magnetic field so the flux linking it changes and an emf is induced; emf is maximum when the coil is parallel to the field and zero when perpendicular; after each half turn the sides move through the field in the opposite direction so the emf reverses, and slip rings pass this AC to the circuit

questions.text: Distinguish between an AC generator and a DC generator in terms of construction and output.
questions.markScheme: AC generator uses slip rings, DC generator uses a split-ring commutator; AC output reverses direction (sine wave), DC output varies but always has the same direction

questions.context: A lamp is rated 60 W, 230 V.
questions.text: Calculate the current in the lamp and its resistance when operating normally.

questions.context: A transformer steps the 230 V mains down to 12 V. Its primary coil has 2300 turns.
questions.text: Calculate the number of turns on the secondary coil.
questions.markScheme: $N_s = N_p \times V_s/V_p$; $N_s = 2300 \times 12/230 = 120$ turns

questions.context: The transformer in 15b is ideal and supplies a 12 V, 36 W lamp.
questions.text: Calculate the current in the secondary coil and in the primary coil.

questions.context: A real transformer draws 0.50 A from the 230 V mains and delivers 8.5 A at 12 V.
questions.text: Calculate the efficiency of the transformer.
questions.markScheme: $P_{in} = 115$ W and $P_{out} = 102$ W; efficiency $= 102/115 \times 100 = 88.7\%$
